paragraphs.text: The idea of proportion comes into these two scriptures. God is a God of order. He is not a God of disorder (1 Corinthians 14: 33), and He is the God of measure (2 Corinthians 10: 13).

We might say He is a God who delights in proportion. The God of measure measures everything. All God’s dealings are measured, even with each one of us individually. There are certain difficulties, burdens and sorrows we have to bear but they are all measured; no one is called upon to suffer without the God of measure entering into it, and there is no suffering laid upon the believer without there being abundance of grace to meet it. There is never a measure of sorrow or burden beyond the grace that God is pleased to supply to meet that sorrow, whatever it may be. It is fine to think of, and to know, the God of measure.
Everything is measured and everything is proportioned.
This first scripture speaks about the incense: “in like proportions shall it be”. It says

“according to the proportions of it” in verse 37. What precedes the incense is the anointing oil. The anointing oil is also in certain proportions. The anointing oil comes down, it is upon persons who are anointed, but the incense arises. In a sense the incense is the answer to God from the anointing. Both the anointing oil and the incense speak of the Spirit, especially as the Spirit of Christ. No matter what is laid upon any one of us there is sufficient in the anointing to help us through in dignity and power. Then the answer is the incense. The anointing oil was put upon the whole tabernacle, but then the incense is what arises, a kind of answer, a response to what comes down. The Spirit came down at Pentecost, and the Spirit is available, as the Spirit of Christ, for every one of us for whatever is laid upon us. The Spirit of Christ is available to us for support and help, and for power and dignity, for God’s glory.

But the incense is what is found here for God’s pleasure in what ascends. It is the grace of Christ expressed. It was seen perfectly in the Lord Jesus when He was here. Think of the proportion of the graces seen in our Lord Jesus Christ. The dependent Man, the subject One, the obedient One, and yet the faithful One. In every situation faithful, and yet along with it, dependent, humble. Beautiful graces shone in the Lord Jesus here in perfect proportion. It has been said that there was not one outstanding feature in the manhood of our Lord Jesus Christ.
That same spirit is to be taken on by us, so that there is proportion, things are proportioned.

As helped in the Lord’s dealings with us, in instruction and in discipleship, by being attached to our Lord Jesus Christ and helped by the Spirit, we are meant to take on these gracious features which are seen perfectly in Him. God is pleased to use discipline too. He passes us through discipline, through sorrows and difficulties, but the end in view is that there should be some feature of the incense. It suggests prayer, how we pray. It is all for the pleasure of God. There is this idea of proportion in it, dear brethren, which I would be concerned about

myself. There may be outstanding features with us, but then the proportion suggests an evenness that is to be arrived at by the Lord’s gracious dealings with us, including His discipline. We learn much by instruction, but we learn much by discipline, by things which we have to go through, things we would rather not go through, things we would rather not have to face. Yet the Lord uses these that there might be proportion in our moral being which is so pleasing to God Himself.
Now in Romans 12 we again have this idea of proportion. The human body is proportioned.
There is no member outstanding in the human body; it is perfectly proportioned. Each belongs to the other, each belongs to the whole. The idea of proportion makes one whole.

Paul writes here about one body having many members, but all the members have not the same office. That is, there is variety but it is all proportioned. In the human body there are a great variety of members, more than I could enumerate. You think of the different systems that operate in the human body—the respiratory system, the nervous system, the blood system. How much operates and each system helps the other, it is all proportioned; and so it is in the one body in Christ. This is meant to work out locally. There is meant to be proportion, making for unity and making for one complete whole, and every member is needed. Any member is missed if it is not functioning. Every member is needed in the local setting, and it speaks in verse 3 about each one having a measure of faith, “as God has dealt to each a measure of faith”. That is the God of measure, proportioning what is needed in the body. It comes down to the locality. God proportions what is needed in the locality. Every one is needed, but then no one dominates; the whole thing works smoothly—that is, the idea of the

body is meant to be expressed locally. In 1 Corinthians 12 Paul speaks about the body. He speaks about the one body, which would be a universal idea involving every believer who has the Spirit of Christ, but then he comes down to “Ye are Christ’s body (verse 27). The assembly at Corinth was meant to express the features that were seen in the body universally.
The body features work locally.

So it goes on to say here, “We, being many, are one body in Christ, and each one members one of the other”. Members of the body of Christ and members one of the other. Each one is necessary. Each one belongs to the other. It is not only the working of love, it is something organic. It is a question of belonging to one another. The human body is, I suppose, one of the most wonderful organisms that there is; but then the body of Christ is a more wonderful organism because it is not physical; it is spiritual, it is animated by the Spirit of Christ—a wonderful organism! We are members one of the other. “But having different gifts, according to the grace that has been given to us, whether it be prophecy, let us prophesy according to the proportion of faith”. Each one has a measure of faith, and each one has a proportion of, faith, and as we function in that proportion it makes for unity and oneness, a smoothness, all for the pleasure of God and for the edifying of one another. May the Lord help us to be attracted by this idea of proportion, to find out what our proportion is, and to fit in in that proportion for the glory and pleasure of God.

articles.title: FAITHFUL MANHOOD
articles.author: C. F. Dadd
articles.place: Words in meeting for ministry, Plainfield, N.J.

paragraphs.text: The intent, dear brethren, in referring to these scriptures is to bring to our attention what can be worked out and brought to completion in our localities, as it is set on by a faithful man.

Nehemiah represents a faithful man, a faithful brother, in a locality. The Spirit of God does not draw to our attention that he had gift, or that he had an outstanding place in service, but what is brought to our attention is that on the principle of faith and love for Jerusalem someone is able to set on something that would result in glary to God and the strengthening and building up of things locally. We had a touch on the Lord’s day as to the thought of completion, things getting through to a finish; and one thing we have noted as we have read together is that under Nehemiah’s direction and lead as a faithful man the wall is completed. The gates are set up, things are brought to a finished idea as to the principle of fellowship. You might say it has a universal bearing, but then too we are to see how it works out in a locality. That is a test to us. We are always tested as to how things work out locally, where we are known to the brethren, where we know each other, where confidence is to be stimulated and strengthened in each other, where the feature of affection is to be seen operating. “By this shall all know that ye are disciples of mine, if ye have love amongst yourselves”, John 13: 35.

So Nehemiah sets on the thought of one who had love for Jerusalem, who was concerned .about Jerusalem, which in our own day would be our peculiar affection for the assembly. He is concerned when he hears the report as to how things were in Jerusalem; and when he goes and takes a look at the city, at the devastation that had come in, the walls broken down, things were in a pitiful condition. He evaluates the whole matter. He takes a look at things and he has the feelings of God as to the city. Beloved, it is a great thing to develop in the feelings of God in relation to matters as they pertain to the assembly. So he says, “Ye see the distress that we are in, that Jerusalem lies waste, its gates are burned with fire. Come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem; that we be no more a reproach”. As we start the week, we begin with the thought of completion, the perfect completion of the work of Christ, and as you proceed in the week you have a sense of what divine Persons have worked out from their own side.
But then it comes over to our side, dear brethren, as to how we are going to work things out, in the week as responsible persons. Now this week for us, in this city, is one of much activity.

We have much in the way of meetings before us. We have much laid out in our households where brethren need to be cared for, but we are not to lose sight of the fact that this week is to proceed in such a way that, as we come to the end of it, the idea of what is finished and complete should mark it. I believe that is the intention of the Lord Jesus that each week we should get through to something definite and complete. So there is the idea of what is working out in our own souls individually and what is working out amongst us collectively.

Nehemiah makes an appeal, “Come, and let us build” and then there is an answer from persons who are prepared to be affected by the lead of one who is faithful. It is not a question of gift. It is really a question of faithfulness, of devotion, of love, and this can be seen in any one of us according to our proportion, according to our measure. Each has not the same measure.

We all have different measures; we have different measures of faith, but the thing can be set on according to the measure that we have. Nehemiah is setting it on according to the measure of faithful manhood which we would have as an objective—the faithfulness of matured manhood. He affects others, so they say, “Let us rise up and build. And they strengthened their hands for the good work”. Well, we want to get strengthened for the good work as we proceed in this week. We have had the Lord’s day. We have had the prayer meeting, which has been called the power meeting. We had a sense of power as we proceeded in that meeting, but it is to give us power in testimony in the course of the week, and in view of our other assemblings, such as tonight.

Then we have this man Eliashib the high priest. He rose up with his brethren and they built the sheep-gate. Here is a priestly man coming into operation and this is to be seen in our locality. The feature of priestliness is coming in and setting in motion something that is going to affect priestliness in the saints so that there is this building going on. Something is being restored. Oh it is a great thing that as these beloved men laboured the wall was being restored. Things were being rebuilt. Historically we can take it back no doubt to how things functioned and were revived in Mr. Darby’s time, and how they have come through. Yet we have to humbly say that, since that time, how much breakdown there has been. Much weakness has come in. But at a time like this a man like Nehemiah would direct our attention to how we can rebuild, how we can restore.

Priestliness comes into this in a very distinct way, so that as priestly features are operating amongst us we are thinking for God. According to our measure we are able to act for God and act like God. That would be the way a priest would function. And what does he do? He affects the rest of the priests, the priestly element, so they rise up and build. It is interesting that they built the sheep-gate and moved on until the time arrived when the wall was finished.

What a moment that was! The principles of fellowship were restored, were rebuilt. The wall was there. It was set up in faithfulness. It took much labour. You look at those chapters and you can see how much labour it took. But they all worked together, and that is what we need.

We need to be all pulling together in our localities, working side by side, with the trowel and the sword (see Nehemiah 4: 17, 18) all in view of the restoration, the rebuilding of this great thought of the wall, involving primarily the thought of the fellowship and the principles of the fellowship. Paul opened up that side; the fellowship of God’s Son; the fellowship of His death; the fellowship of the Spirit; fellowship with one another. Here they arrive at what is finished. What a great matter that is, that the principles of the fellowship, in that sense, are finished, they are recognised, they are accepted, they are carried by us and they are maintained by us.

It goes on to say that “it came to pass when the wall was built, and I had set up the doors, that the doorkeepers and the singers and the Levites were appointed”. You can see that what is in view is that there is going to be something peculiarly secured for God. There are going to be the doorkeepers, but there are going to be the singers, there are going to be the Levites. What we find is that things are primarily recovered and secured for the

pleasure of divine Persons. We come into it in the way that we fit into matters, the way we fit into things locally, the joys that we have, the way God brings us into joy. Joy is a known thing in this book, in this great thought of recovery—the joy of Jerusalem. But the prime thought, beloved, is that the great thoughts of God are secured, the rebuilding, the reclaiming of things, is secured for the glory of God. Let us have that ever in our hearts that the prime question in christianity is what is for divine Persons, and as we labour at things and work together locally, we get through to what is complete, what is finished. So we want to be looking for this as we proceed in this week. There is going to be much. We have been praying much about it. We are going to be looking for something complete and finished to be arrived at in our histories individually and collectively under the eye of God. And it will be that which will result in glory; it will minister to the affections of, divine Persons, dear brethren, and I believe that is the greatest thing that we can have part in. May we be strengthened for this, for His name’s sake.
The Spirit has stressed amongst us these days the need for our affections being engaged with what we have considered together. I feel simply that I

want to continue that because one of the safeguards against departure is to have the affections livingly engaged, and it also enables you to undertake the sacrificial side of christianity. I wanted to draw from these scriptures to show that in the mighty men we have typified affection for Christ; in Urijah the Hittite affection for the testimony of God; in Jacob affection for the local assembly, and in Paul his love of the truth and how the truth so engaged his affections that he was prepared to enter into what must have been to him one of the most testing conflicts in his ministerial career.

These three mighty men, of course, are enshrined in heaven’s annals. They are often spoken about, but it is quite apparent that what motivated this wondrous act of devotion was their affection for David. No doubt they had benefited by his victories; they had been affected by his movements; they had seen the grace of his spirit, his patience, and his loyalty and fidelity to those who rallied round him. Affection, beloved brethren, is something that has to be generated, and as you contemplate Christ, as you ponder His moral worth and His beauty, the Spirit generates a deep affection for Him.

The Spirit of God comments that it was the harvest time. Many choice positive applications have been made of the fact that it was the harvest time but I trust that for the occasion the brethren will bear with my application. No doubt these men could have legitimately occupied themselves with the harvest. At harvest time, I understand, in the old economy, every man had to be at his work; it was a feature of dwelling in the land that, as the harvest came round, every man had to be at his work—they had a legitimate reason for being in the harvest field at that time. You see, business is one of

the most legitimate reasons. The need to earn a living and provide for yourself and your dependents is legitimate. But these men let the fields lie ungathered as far as they were concerned in the urgency of the moment and what it called for in their expression of love for David.
He was down, at Adullam and the troop of the Philistines encamped in the valley of Rephaim.
“And David was then in the stronghold; and the Philistines’ garrison was then at Bethlehem”.

Now they had garrisoned it; they did not leave a few old people to look after Bethlehem, they garrisoned it—some indication of the spiritual power of wickedness which the enemy would deploy in order to withstand anything that is going to yield something for Christ. And that garrison presented in itself something quite formidable for these men. “And David longed”—

he gave expression to this deep desire that was in his heart—“… give me to drink of the water of the well of Bethlehem, which is in the gate!”. Mr. Taylor often in his ministry drew attention to this sort of request; the request of Elijah in 1 Kings 17: 13, “But make me thereof a little cake first …”—the natural heart reacts and says, What selfishness! But he pointed out that when the claims of Christ come in in that way, He is testing out what is there in affection for Himself and for the truth.

The very character of the request is a test in itself because the human mind can construe it otherwise. They might have said, ‘David, do you know the odds? Do you know what the odds are—a whole garrison and only three of us? Could you not forgo your drink until the odds are different?’. They did not say that, beloved brethren. Oh what a test that is! We count the odds; we think that, well, circumstances may alter and then I can more readily

meet the requirements of Christ; but they did not hesitate. It says they “broke through the camp of the Philistines, and drew water out of the well of Bethlehem, which is in the gate, and took it, and brought it to David”. I have often wondered how they carried it. How would you carry it today? “But we have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Corinthians 4: 7)—your body, beloved brethren, your spirit, your affections; that is the way you carry the water from the well of Bethlehem to David; that is how they carried it. Will you carry it, you young people?—that body a living sacrifice on the altar—will you carry it? will you carry the water to David? will you satisfy His heart? Oh, the Lord recognises with deep feeling the sacrificial character of such an act. He says, ‘It is worthy of God; it is a sacrifice of the highest order, a drink offering’, and he pours it out. I would say to my younger brethren, The Lord values your affection. He would, so to speak, in the quality of it use it as something that can yield delight and pleasure to the heart of God.
So in regard to Urijah we might see in him affection for the testimony. I have often pondered as to what Urijah would think when he got the recall from the battlefield. Would he say,

‘What is behind this?’. Beloved brethren, the day you feel that you have got a recall from the battlefield, ask yourself what is behind it. The testimony is involved, and there is no recall from the battlefield in that sense. “A good soldier of Jesus Christ”—that is what Paul says to Timothy (2 Timothy 2: 3). Urijah must have wondered; to be recalled from the battlefield, and Israel and Judah dwelling in booths, and Joab and the servants encamped in the open fields. O, beloved, the enemy is behind every suggestion that weakens the rigours of the testimonial conflict. The testimony

is a constant matter; it is not only a matter of meetings; the testimony of the Lord is a constant matter and we in this sense are never away from the battlefield. What comes out in Urijah is his intense love for the testimony. He would not take up what was legitimate—there it was, his house, but in the urgency of matters he maintained his fidelity to the testimony.
You get in the passage a sense that he loved the testimony. Do we love the testimony? Some may sceptically say, ‘How can you speak about the testimony? Look at the history of things’.

Beloved, the testimony of God remains; it will remain until the end. It will be carried on in its purity by men like Urijah, men like Paul, men like Timothy—are we amongst them? Are we prepared, even if we are placed in a position that we cannot explain circumstantially, to keep before us the testimony of God, the ark, Judah, and Israel? What enables you to do so?—
affection for the testimony of God. Despite the outward smallness of things, there is enshrined in many hearts a love for the testimony of God.

Jacob demonstrates love for his wife, or—which I suppose would be a just application—the local assembly, and his affection for her sustained him in his rigorous service. As he recounts it later, he said his wages were changed ten times, “in the day the heat consumed me, and the frost by night”, Genesis 31: 40. You know, when you love your local assembly, you get these experiences—the heat by day—circumstances that are overpowering; the frost by night—love waxing cold; but you have to go through it, heat and cold; seven years you have to go through it, and then you find that what you get is not what you expected. When Leah came on to his vision that morning he did not say, ‘Oh, it has not been worth it’—no, he did not say that; the scripture does not say that he despised Leah. He

was disappointed, but he made the best of her. Oh what grace it needs, beloved brethren, sometimes to make the best of things—in your local position to make the best of Leah and sacrificially devote yourself these extra seven years for Rachel your heart’s desire, your ideal!

Have you an ideal? You will never sacrifice unless you have an ideal. Keep the ideal in front of you, despite all the vicissitudes of the cold and heat and the change in your wages (no unions to negotiate for you, none at all!). It was not always an increase Jacob got, but he went on, and what strengthened him was his affection for his local assembly typically. Could I not leave that word with you, brethren? How are we going to proceed? I think we can only proceed as there is a deep affection for our local assembly, and a willingness to sacrifice in labour and love amongst them.

With Paul in Galatians it was love for the truth. It is quite a remarkable expression in an epistle like this, “I am crucified with Christ, and no longer live, I, but Christ lives in me; but in that I now live in flesh, I live by faith, the faith of the Son of God, who has loved me and given himself for me”. Paul said in effect, ‘Nothing will shake me in my affection for the truth, because I have a link with the blessed Man who brought all this wondrous light and blessing to my soul’; “the Son of God, who has loved me and given himself for me”. It was no light matter for Paul to face Peter (see Galatians 2: 14). The historical account breathes the meekness and lowliness of Christ. He established the great principle that the love of the truth is more important than the love of the brethren. Do we accept that? What a test it is that the love of the truth is more important than the love of the brethren! And how can you take that stance? You can only take it if you can say in measure like Paul,
“… the Son of God, who has loved me and given himself for me”.

Paul announced the blessings of the gospel on the principle of grace, and he would withstand everything that would militate against the character of the dispensation. You know, conflicts come up, tests come up, and we try to analyse the issue and the situation mentally. In the assembly, beloved brethren, no situation can be analysed mentally; you cannot analyse anything that happens in the divine realm on that principle. You must search by the Spirit as to what is moral, and what morally bears on the issue that the Lord is raising. That is what Paul saw in this matter with Peter. He saw that underneath this issue there was what was moral in this respect, that the foundations of the gospel were being undermined through respect of persons. So conflicts arise, and we are tested. We can refer to ministry and quote precedents, things right in themselves, but there is the guidance the Spirit gives you on account of the place the truth has in your affections. We are less liable to go wrong when we are guided thus, that the truth of the gospel was sacrificially secured by the Son of God who loved us and gave Himself for us.
The people of God have a great heritage, sacrificially bought at great cost. May our affections be increasingly engaged and thus stimulated in like sacrificial service, for His name’s sake.

The history of Jacob is familiar to us all. We are, perhaps, as well acquainted with Jacob as we are with anybody in the Scriptures. We have recently in the sub-division taken account of the way in which God first lets him learn lessons in a hard school and then takes him in hand and refines and polishes him until at the end Jacob cannot help shining. This point of which we have read is a critical point in Jacob’s history; he is really on his way to returning, I suppose. He is met first of all by the angels of God and comes into Esau’s territory; he prepares a gift for Esau and then he has this crisis of the night and has to wrestle with God.
While it refers to the angel, he, says, “I have seen God face to face”.

So that the time here is one where Jacob is learning deep lessons and he is learning things as they are before God, a place where I think we learn our lessons best in relation to whatever sphere they apply to. In this chapter he sees Esau coming with four hundred men. What I am impressed by and what I wish to say a word about now—bearing on exercise and, I could even say, concern which I myself carry and I believe the brethren would—is what seems to be the instinctive way in which Jacob protects his wives and his children. I think that comes out here in a very distinctive way. He puts them in a certain order, the maidservants and their children,

and then Leah and her children, then Rachel and Joseph, and then he goes before them. I think that Jacob’s instinct is to protect his wives and the children. I venture to suggest, beloved, that that is a thing as to which exercise is needed in the present day, as to whether the saints generally, brothers generally, are concerned to protect their wives and their children.

I refer to this because of things to which I may refer, but Esau, on the one hand, represents Jacob’s brother whom years earlier Jacob had himself wronged, and therefore there was, to say the very least, an embarrassing situation to be faced in this chapter; that is one side of it.

But on the other hand Esau represents a profane person who for one meal despised his birthright. I think in that sense, beloved, he may for us represent the character of the world as profane, the character of the world—which has despised blessing which God had in view, despised it actually in Christ, in Christ rejected. The epistle to the Hebrews brings out the way in which Esau is to be viewed, not just in relation to the brotherly covenant on Jacob’s part, but in relation to the place that Esau stands in as representing the world in, really morally, one of its worst characters. We may be inclined to think that the moral character of the world is best illustrated in its lust and such things, but the real character of the world is that it is profane, that is, that it has not liked to retain God in its knowledge and it goes on with God in Christ rejected, God in Christ finding no place in the world. Jacob comes before us as one who would protect his wives and his children in relation to such as world as that.
I think, beloved, that is a needed exercise in the present day, and I relate it to a practical thing, the concern which I think would-be widespread

as to a tendency which is developing for married sisters to go to work. I speak quite plainly about this because this is what I have in mind. I think that the Lord might raise with us all the question whether there is that disposition amongst us generally which believes that our wives should be protected by not being exposed to the world in its profanity by being led or allowed or permitted— perhaps even of their own will—to go into the world when the place for the believer’s wife is in the house, which she is to rule. The Lord would revive some of these things with us. He would promote exercise with us.

I raise these things not conscious that they exist in this city, but as was prayed here last night, the Lord would be active in speaking in a place to speak in relation to things among the saints universally. And I believe that exercise needs to be promoted as to this tendency to which I refer and that if there was that state of exercise among the saints as to it and a disposition not to be neglectful of it, we would find that something was asserted among the saints which without any interdiction had the effect of preventing what I believe is not intended to be a thing which exists in a believer’s household. As the brethren know, or would realise, I do not here need to dwell on what I might speak of as legitimate exceptions to these things. If one begins to dwell on the exceptions one finds that one has constructed a wall made of loopholes; the exceptions speak for themselves, but the principle is what we would be concerned with.
Jacob here is concerned to protect his wives. He goes before them in the face of Esau, as I say Esau not merely representing a brother who might be resentful—we would need to be protective in that
regard—but Esau representing the world in its profanity. Therefore, beloved, would the Lord speak to us to stimulate us in exercise about this kind of thing?

Then he is not only careful to protect his wives, but he is careful to protect his children. In each case it says he put the maidservants and their children, and Leah and her children, and Rachel and Joseph—the only child that Rachel had at this time—hindmost. I do not dwell on the order in which he put them, that could be dwelt on at another time, but what Jacob does is to put himself in the exposed position. In a sense, beloved, the husband is the only one who needs to be in such an exposed position. Brothers have to go into the world in order to make a living and to earn what is righteously required according as the Lord may provide for them, but it is Jacob who has to go on before and the wives and the children are behind, but they are protected because Jacob has himself taken up the exposed position. Let us bear in mind that Jacob protects not only the wives, he protects the children. I suggest to the brethren that again it would be a matter of exercise whether we should expose our children to the world and in particular to its education until the age at which this is lawfully required in the country.

One views with concern the tendency, and an increasing tendency, for little children to be sent out to schools, nursery schools, day schools, play groups, whatever they may be called, at a time when one would expect that they would still be affectionately in the care of their mother. Why should it not be so, why should anything different be thought? If, as Jacob says later in the chapter, “My lord knows that the children are tender”, we took account of that, who would want to expose them into the

world before it was required? I can well remember in regard to my own children, when my older boy first went to school, having the impression that he would never to the same extent be in our care again as he had been up to that time. Would we not desire to keep our children within our own care for as long as we legally can? It may be said that they are lonely, or that they need company, or that it is an advantage to begin to read, and so on. But the christian household has resources for these things.

Jacob says, “My lord knows that the children are tender”. We know that the children are tender, we know it very well. If we thought we were sending a child at three or four out into the world, we would keep it at home—it is because they go into an environment which is legitimated even by a provision of the government and by the pattern of society in the present day. It does not make them right for the believer. I think we need to bear in mind that the children are tender. They are tender for a long time, certainly still tender when they are five, but they are at least beginning to be capable of moving in the sphere in which they then have to move.

Would we not desire that we should be like Jacob and be ourselves in the exposed position in order that the children and the wives may be protected? Jacob says, “My lord knows that the children are tender”. But he also says, “and the suckling sheep and kine are with me”. That is to say, he is really looking at the mothers again, that is what Jacob is looking at. He is still looking in the area of the wives and the children and wants to protect them, not now from exposure to the world in its profanity, as Esau represents it, but from the arduousness of the journey. He says, “Let my lord, I pray thee, pass on before his servant”. He says to Esau,
‘You go on at your own pace’. Let the world go on at

its own pace, and I will come, he says, “at my ease according to the pace of the cattle that is before me, and according to the pace of the children”. That is to say, Jacob is going to remain protective as long as protection is needed.

One is not surprised to find in David’s history that God took him “from following the suckling-ewes”, Psalm 78: 71. That is to say, David was like Jacob, he was in the area where he protected things and what is tender. Think of the word to Peter as to the sheep and the lambs. Jacob is a man in whom we find many elements of our own history and our own characteristics, but I suggest that we would do well to find this character of Jacob’s in ourselves, that is that we will protect the wives and the children. I express these things to the beloved brethren as having carried concern about them for quite a long time, but I sometimes feel that we hesitate too long to speak about matters which really have a certain gravity of their own. As we sat, and to be simple, no other brother spoke, I referred to the scripture which came to my mind as bearing on that exercise which I carry.
Praise be to God my Maker
Who giveth songs by night.
‘Tis oft nocturnal season
In life’s brief way below,
But every night a reason
The coming day will show.
His chast’ning hand seems heavy,
So oft misunderstood,
Demands betimes a levy
Beyond what seemeth good.
Arrest, my soul, such thinking!
Thy pathway all is planned;
Lift up thyself from sinking,
It is the Father’s hand.
The Father who has called thee,
Thy spirit moulds with care,
His pleasure now to test thee
And see more fruit appear.
No son delights in scourging,
‘Tis grievous at the time,
But consequent on purging
The fruit is rendered prime.
And so, most tender Father,
Thee always will I praise,
Spring, summer, autumn, winter,
In nights as well as days.
It is Thy love transcending,
Behind Thine unkenned ways,
That holds the heart low bending,
Ensures the constant lays.
Praise be to God my Maker
Who giveth songs by night.
London

DIVINE ASSURANCE Many of the Psalms reflect the simple, confiding relations which David enjoyed with Jehovah. In Psalm 35, written in a time of much adversity, he says to Him, “Say unto my soul, I am thy salvation”. With child-like simplicity he asks Jehovah to speak this word of comfort to him. How ready divine Persons are to give us such assurances, and at times of difficulty or extremity how precious it is to receive them. We can think of the word to Abram, “Fear not, Abram; I am thy shield, thy exceeding great reward” (Genesis 15: 1); to Joshua, “As I was with Moses, so will I be with thee” (Joshua 1: 5), and to Paul, “Fear not … because I am with thee” (Acts 18: 9). What strength these words must have given to these great men, and we may experience the same reassurance as seeking to be here for the will of God in an adverse scene.

Christ has accomplished redemption, but more has come to light than that, and that is, God has been declared, and you can strike your roots deeper and deeper in the revelation of God, which has been given to us in Christ.
